reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with chronic or intermittent watery, non-bloody diarrhoea, often with urgency, nocturnal stools, mild weight loss and abdominal cramps
Predominantly affects middle-aged and older women
The endoscopic appearance of the colon is usually normal, so the diagnosis depends entirely on histology from biopsies
The defining feature is a thickened subepithelial collagen band beneath the surface epithelium, distinguishing it from lymphocytic colitis
Associated with autoimmune conditions such as coeliac disease and thyroid disease, and with drugs including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and proton-pump inhibitors
Random biopsies should be taken from several segments because histological changes can be patchy and are often more pronounced in the right colon
Budesonide for microscopic colitis is the mainstay of treatment, alongside stopping culprit drugs
reference.pathophysiology: Collagenous colitis is a form of microscopic colitis in which the colonic mucosa appears macroscopically normal but shows a characteristic thickened subepithelial band of collagen together with increased chronic inflammatory cells in the lamina propria and surface epithelial injury. The mechanism is thought to involve an abnormal mucosal immune response to luminal antigens, including drugs and possibly bile acids, in genetically predisposed individuals, leading to altered fluid and electrolyte handling and a secretory, watery diarrhoea. The thickened collagen band, rather than being purely structural, reflects abnormal subepithelial fibroblast activity.
additionalInvestigations: Colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy with multiple segmental biopsies despite normal mucosa
Histological measurement of the subepithelial collagen band thickness
Coeliac serology and thyroid function tests
Medication review for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and proton-pump inhibitors
redFlags: Bloody diarrhoea, which is atypical and should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
Significant unintentional weight loss requiring exclusion of malignancy or coeliac disease
Severe dehydration or electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhoea
New iron-deficiency anaemia suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and does not carry an increased colorectal cancer risk; symptoms often respond well to treatment, although relapse after stopping therapy is common and some patients require maintenance treatment.
pitfalls: Labelling the patient as irritable bowel syndrome and not taking biopsies of normal-looking mucosa
Taking biopsies from only one colonic segment and missing patchy disease
Failing to review and stop drugs that can trigger or perpetuate the condition
Confusing it with lymphocytic colitis rather than distinguishing by the collagen band
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
British Society of Gastroenterology guidance on microscopic colitis
management: Induce remission with oral budesonide as first-line therapy
Withdraw implicated drugs, particularly non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and proton-pump inhibitors
Symptomatic relief of mild disease with antidiarrhoeals such as loperamide
Consider a bile-acid sequestrant such as colestyramine where bile-acid malabsorption contributes
Identify and treat associated coeliac disease and thyroid dysfunction
Low-dose maintenance budesonide for frequent relapse, reserving immunomodulators or biologics for refractory disease
Advise smoking cessation and arrange gastroenterology follow-up given the relapsing course
